subjects.displayTitle: The power and sovereignty of God: He doeth whatsoever He willeth
subjects.introduction: What do the Writings mean when they call God all-powerful, and how is a believer to live with that knowledge? These 300 chosen quotations include every verified authorized selection in the compilation. They begin with a sovereignty that has no beginning or end and with the creative Word that calls all things into being, then consider the freedom of the divine will, the weakness of every created power before it, and the forbearance and hidden wisdom with which that power is exercised. Later readings follow the same power as it appears in the Manifestation of God, in Bahá’u’lláh’s sovereignty while a prisoner, in the invincibility of His Cause, in the passing of earthly kings and in His dominion over hearts. The guide ends with healing and protection, with longer prayers of supplication, and with the refrain Potent art Thou that closes so many prayers. Most passages are prayers and Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh, joined by writings of the Báb and by Tablets and reported talks of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá; two supplied renderings of authorized prayers follow at the end with their catalogue status.
subjects.arc: Sovereignty without beginning or end → Creation and the creative Word → He doeth whatsoever He willeth → The mighty humbled, the lowly raised → Forbearance, justice and hidden wisdom → The power revealed in His Manifestation → Sovereign though a prisoner → None can frustrate His purpose → Kings and the passing of earthly rule → Dominion over the hearts → Healing, protection and aid → Supplication to the All-Powerful → “Potent art Thou”: the refrain of prayer

Read together, these passages ask what it means for a power to be complete in itself and still to be exercised.

These readings look for God’s power in the created world and in the Word that brings it into being. The Báb speaks of God calling all things into being by His injunction “Be”, and of God being at every moment engaged in a wondrous work and a new creation. Bahá’u’lláh marvels at the power that makes spring and autumn appear at a single time and produces light from fire and joy from sorrow, says that all the atoms of the earth bear witness to that power, and challenges those who claim lordship to produce a single bubble upon the water. In reported talks ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes that no one could create a single grain, that all created things are captive to the law of nature except the divine power, and that God brings fire from stone and flowers from black dust. The section ends with the Word itself: the heavens may vanish, but what the Pen has revealed shall never pass away, and one verse outweighs the treasuries of all creation.

In reported talks ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes that no one could create a single grain, that all created things are captive to the law of nature except the divine power, and that God brings fire from stone and flowers from black dust. The section ends with the Word itself: the heavens may vanish, but what the Pen has revealed shall never pass away, and one verse outweighs the treasuries of all creation.

These readings dwell on the phrase that recurs throughout the subject: He doeth whatsoever He willeth. Bahá’u’lláh writes that God bestows His favor on whom He wills and takes it from whom He wills, that the Will of God has triumphed over the will of His creatures, and that not a leaf stirs save by His leave. He adds that God has not desired that every soul should do whatever it wills, and that all He ordains is for the good of His servants. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the servant can do nothing of his own will alone, that the pen of destiny is in the hand of divine decree and not of human design, and that if creation went forward by only one rule the all-encompassing Power could not make itself felt. Other passages qualify how this is understood: Bahá’u’lláh says that every matter has its appointed time and that divine decrees work through means and causes, and a reported talk compares God to the Captain of a ship whose mate is the Covenant.

He adds that God has not desired that every soul should do whatever it wills, and that all He ordains is for the good of His servants. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the servant can do nothing of his own will alone, that the pen of destiny is in the hand of divine decree and not of human design, and that if creation went forward by only one rule the all-encompassing Power could not make itself felt. Other passages qualify how this is understood: Bahá’u’lláh says that every matter has its appointed time and that divine decrees work through means and causes, and a reported talk compares God to the Captain of a ship whose mate is the Covenant.

These readings set the power of God beside the weakness of everything else. In prayer after prayer Bahá’u’lláh confesses that every possessor of greatness is as nothing before God’s greatness, that the mighty have acknowledged their weakness and the learned their ignorance, that every conqueror is but a serf whom His hand has subjected, and that even the holy Ones and the Prophets confess their helplessness before the revelations of His might. His prayers have the believer testify to his own powerlessness and poverty before God’s might and wealth, and the Báb writes, Say, God is the Lord and all are worshippers unto Him. The same power also lifts up. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that when the Omnipotent Lord glances upon a powerless servant, that servant becomes a mine of might; a reported talk says the aid of the Most High turns a drop into an ocean and a gnat into an eagle; and Bahá’u’lláh says His might can raise a straw to the galaxies while returning the possessors of palaces to their graves.

These readings ask why a God of such power allows what He allows. Bahá’u’lláh calls God the One Whose strength is immense and Whose decree is terrible, Who deals equitably with all in heaven and on earth and causes men to die through His wrath, and the Báb speaks of the Day of Severing when He shall judge through the power of Truth. Yet most of the section concerns His forbearance. A prayer of Bahá’u’lláh marvels at God’s patience despite His power and His forbearance despite His might; another says that His forbearance with the idolaters is due to a wisdom concealed from His servants; and Bahá’u’lláh says that had not His mercy preceded all things, He would have returned existence to nothingness. The Báb writes that delay in a decree for the loved ones is no sign of impotence, nor is respite for the enemy a sign of restraint. In a reported talk ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that God is not impotent and could remove every barrier, but that great wisdom is concealed in sufferings which only the pure-hearted discern.

These readings turn from God’s power over creation to the power revealed through His Manifestation. In the Súriy-i-Haykal God addresses the Living Temple, placing in His right hand the empire of all things and ordaining Him the source of all existence in the new creation, that all may know His power to accomplish what He has purposed through His word “Be”. Other passages say that God, not men, selects the Promised One, and that were He to pronounce black to be white, none may ask wherefore or why.

These readings concern a power that appeared in what looked like its opposite. Bahá’u’lláh writes that if absolute power appears in the garment of powerlessness, and the Absolute Sovereign appears as one ruled and oppressed, there is wisdom in it; that a glory no abasement can approach has shone forth from the horizon of the prison; and that without armies, means or weapons He summoned all to God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that though imprisoned He was the Ruler of what was and what would be, and that though alone and forsaken He subdued the realm of being. Recorded and reported accounts add particulars. Bahá’u’lláh’s own words recall that He stayed in Tihran amid danger because God willed to manifest His Cause. A reported talk recalls that the governor of ‘Akká sought permission to see the Prisoner for years. In Paris ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells His hearers that they see the powers of God, for He is no longer in prison but talking with them.

These readings gather the assurance that nothing can frustrate God’s purpose for His Cause. Bahá’u’lláh writes that the more His enemies strive to quench His Light the brighter it will shine, that were all the governments on earth to unite and take His life this Divine Fire would never be quenched, and that neither the grunting and barking of opponents nor the opposition of the hosts of the world can withhold the Almighty from His purpose. He says that God has made the tyranny of oppressors and the dominion of rulers a means of exalting His Word, and that through the blood that was shed the earth has been impregnated with the signs of His might. The Báb writes that God has undisputed triumph over every victorious one. In reported talks ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that nothing can prevent the fulfilment of the Word of God, that the enemies themselves became the cause of the Cause’s exaltation, and that even if they cut Him to pieces the Cause of God will prosper in every way.

These readings describe the kind of dominion God seeks. In the Kitáb-i-Aqdas Bahá’u’lláh tells the kings that it is not His wish to lay hands on their kingdoms, for His mission is to seize and possess the hearts of men, and He bids all observe His commandments for the love of His beauty. Elsewhere He writes that He could have conquered the whole world with a single word, but gave sovereignty to sovereigns and reserved for Himself the love of the hearts of His servants, and that through the Most Exalted Word He took possession of the cities of hearts, burning away their veils. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that a true prince is the soul who conquers the realm of hearts and establishes an eternal, spiritual sovereignty. In reported talks He says that love is the eternal sovereignty and the divine power by which the kings of earth are overcome, that only the divine potency can unite hearts, and that it was the power of God that gathered His hearers in spite of cold and windy weather.

The guide closes with the confession that ends prayer after prayer. Again and again Bahá’u’lláh’s prayers conclude, Potent art Thou to do what Thou willest, followed by names of God: the Help in Peril, the Self-Subsisting, the All-Glorious, the Most Bountiful, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise, He Whose help is implored by all men. The Báb’s prayers close in the same manner. A Tablet of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá ends, Thou art the All-Powerful, the All-Glorious, the Omnipotent, and a prayer in one of His reported talks says, Thou art mighty. Thou art powerful. Thou art the Giver. Gathered together, these short sentences show how the subject of this guide lives inside devotion. After asking for something, the one who prays acknowledges that God is able to grant it and calls on Him by one of His names. Read slowly, the repetition becomes a study of the names themselves, and of what each one says about the power to which the prayer is addressed.

In these authorized words from a prayer of Bahá’u’lláh, the one who prays implores the Lord of all being, Who overshadows all things visible and invisible, by His Name whereby He has subdued the hearts and the souls of men, and by the billows of the Ocean of His mercy and the splendors of the Daystar of His bounty. questions: The readings say that God’s sovereignty has no beginning and that a king without a kingdom is impossible, yet also that God is independent of all things. How do the sections on eternal sovereignty and on creation help you hold these together?

Many passages repeat that He doeth whatsoever He willeth, while others say that every matter has its appointed time and that divine decrees work through means and causes. What does the section on the divine will suggest about the place of human effort, medicine and planning?

Bahá’u’lláh marvels at God’s patience despite His power, and the Báb says that respite for the enemy is no sign of restraint. How do the readings on forbearance respond to the question of why suffering and injustice are allowed to continue?

Bahá’u’lláh writes that absolute power may appear in the garment of powerlessness. Using the accounts of His imprisonment and of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s release, consider what kind of power the section on sovereignty in prison describes.

In the Kitáb-i-Aqdas Bahá’u’lláh says that His mission is to seize and possess the hearts of men, not to lay hands on kingdoms. How do the sections on kings and on hearts change the meaning of the words power and sovereignty?
About a sixth of the guide is the short refrain Potent art Thou to do what Thou willest. Choose one closing name of God from that section and consider how it shapes the prayer it ends.
